## 4. lore — what தெரியும் and சரி actually contain

**ANNA:** what தெரியும் and சரி actually contain

**ANNA:** தெரியும்
> this word — people translate it as 'I know', but that is not quite what it contains.

**ANNA:** it is closer to 'it is visible to me'. the root is about something being perceptible, being clear, being in view. knowing is a side effect of something becoming visible.

**ANNA:** so when someone in Coimbatore says

**ANNA:** யாருக்கு தெரியும்?
> they are not really asking who has the information. they are asking — to whom is this visible? who can see it? it is a softer, more open question than it sounds in English.

**ANNA:** சரி
> this one is old. the root means straight, level, correct — the way a carpenter's line is straight. when something is சரி, it sits right, it is properly aligned.

**ANNA:** சரி சரி
> said twice like this, the alignment has been made. not 'yes yes, fine', more like — okay, it has settled, we can move. there is a little finality in the repetition that the single word does not have.

**ANNA:** சரியாயிடும்
> this form carries the whole arc. it will become straight. it will sort itself out and come right. the 'becoming' is built into the word — it is not fixed yet, but the direction is already there.

**ANNA:** one root about visibility, one about being level. those two ideas are doing a lot of quiet work in ordinary conversation.

## 10. lore — the English words that went native

**ANNA:** the English words that went native

**ANNA:** Two of the most common words at a Tamil table both started somewhere else entirely.

**ANNA:** சூப்பர்
> This one is just the English word super — borrowed whole, kept forever.

**ANNA:** But something happened when it crossed over. In English, super is an intensifier — it modifies something else. Super fast, super good.

**ANNA:** In Coimbatore Tamil it landed as a complete verdict on its own. You taste the idli. You say —

**ANNA:** சூப்பர்
> — and that is the whole sentence. Nothing after it. Nothing needed.

**ANNA:** The borrowing sharpened it. It became more final in Tamil than it ever was in English.

**ANNA:** அவங்க
> This one is older and has more going on inside it.

**ANNA:** The base is a demonstrative — that person, that one over there, someone not standing with you right now.

**ANNA:** But the ending is doing something specific. That -nga you hear at the back — it is the same sound that puts respect into a verb. The word is carrying deference inside its own shape.

**ANNA:** So when you say —

**ANNA:** அவங்க
> — you are not just saying they. You are already signalling that these people are worth your regard. The respect is built in, not added on top.

**ANNA:** One word arrived from outside and got sharper. One word grew the courtesy into its own bones. Both ended up completely at home.

## 16. lore — two small words that carry more than they look like they should

**ANNA:** two small words that carry more than they look like they should

**ANNA:** There is a word that means a little, and the Coimbatore version of it has a kind of tenderness built in that the dictionary does not mention.

**ANNA:** கொஞ்சம்
> konjam — a little

**ANNA:** What it literally holds is something like a small embrace. The root idea is closeness, smallness, something held gently. You hear it in the way a mother talks to a child, in the way someone coaxes rather than commands. When a Coimbatore auntie says eat a little more, she is not measuring food.

**ANNA:** இன்னும் கொஞ்சம் சாப்பிடுங்க
> eat a little more — the word is doing the coaxing

**ANNA:** And when you double it — konjam konjam — it means little by little, slowly, the way something dawns on you. That doubling is a very Tamil move. Repeat a word and you change its dimension, not just its volume.

**ANNA:** கொஞ்சம் கொஞ்சம் புரியுது
> slowly it is becoming clear — not a little, but gradually

**ANNA:** The other word is enakku. On paper it means to me or for me. What it is doing in practice is something closer to staking a claim on an experience — making it personal, making it felt, not just reported.

**ANNA:** எனக்கு புரியல
> it did not reach me — not I don't understand, but understanding did not arrive
